findings.headline: Capital programme is 36% underspent overall at mid-year
findings.detail: Of £58.7m budgeted for 2025-26, only £37.9m has been spent by December. At the halfway point, 64% of planned capital deployment has occurred with £20.8m remaining.
findings.matters: Significant capital programme slippage indicates the council may not deliver planned investment, requiring reforecasting and affecting growth and regeneration plans that support financial sustainability
findings.figures: Total budget £58,747,362, Actual spend £37,935,648, Underspent £20,811,713
findings.quote: TOTAL CAPITAL PROGRAMME 58,747,362  37,935,648  20,811,713

findings.headline: Three major schemes are 89–98% underspent: Leisure, Museum, Crematorium
findings.detail: Leisure Facilities (£8m budgeted, £878k spent), Museum Building Improvements (£2.4m budgeted, £149k spent), and Crematorium Cremator Improvements (£2.5m budgeted, £64k spent) show minimal deployment. Collectively these schemes are £24m behind budget.
findings.matters: Multiple major capital projects with minimal progress at mid-year indicates systemic delivery constraints or unrealistic budget planning that will affect the council's capital strategy
findings.figures: Leisure £8m budgeted vs £878k spent; Museum £2.4m budgeted vs £149k spent; Crematorium £2.5m budgeted vs £64k spent
findings.quote: Leisure Facilities Improvements 8,000,000  877,619  7,122,381; Museum Building Improvements 2,400,000  148,995  2,251,005; Crematorium Cremator Impovements 2,500,000  63,961  2,436,039

findings.headline: Greyfriars capital scheme is 97% underspent at mid-year
findings.detail: Greyfriars, budgeted at £12.2m for 2025-26, has spent only £422k by December. This major capital project has delivered less than 3% of its annual allocation in the first six months.
findings.matters: Minimal progress on a multi-million pound capital project raises questions about scheme viability, planning obstacles, or market conditions that could jeopardise capital programme delivery
findings.figures: Budget £12,200,000, Actual £422,048, Underspent £11,777,952

findings.headline: Kings Quarter is £6.3m over budget at mid-year
findings.detail: The Kings Quarter scheme budgeted at £18m for 2025-26 has already spent £24.3m by December, a 35% cost overrun in the first half of the year. This is the council's largest capital scheme by budget.
findings.matters: Major cost overruns on flagship regeneration projects signal delivery risk and suggest the full business case will be exceeded, directly affecting debt servicing capacity

findings.headline: Waste & Recycling overspent by £395k; Ubico contract performance and historical income loss
findings.detail: The council's largest service overspent by £395k. Part relates to loss of historical shared service income no longer received; the Ubico waste contract has minor pressures being managed. Bulky waste and garden waste performed better than expected.
findings.matters: Waste is typically a council's largest controllable spend. A £395k overspend on a £5.5m budget (7%) suggests either contract cost escalation or demand surge that the council cannot control.
findings.figures: Waste & Recycling £395k overspend on £5.511m budget
findings.quote: Waste & Recycling and Streetcare finished the year £276k over budget. The Ubico contract is regularly monitored and the main variances do not relate to overspend on the main Ubico contract, although there are some minor pressures which are being managed. The majority of the variance relates to a budget for an historical shared service income which is no longer received and was corrected in the 2026-27 budget.

findings.headline: Procurement Act 2023 delays cost £65k+ in lost leisure operator revenue for 2025-26
findings.detail: Freedom Leisure delays caused by new procurement rules have reduced expected revenue by £65k in 2025-26 and will impact 2026-27, with only partial offset from VAT changes.
findings.matters: Leisure revenues are key to many councils' income models. Procurement delays preventing capital works and delaying revenue recovery increase financial uncertainty.
findings.figures: £65k revenue shortfall in 2025-26; £40k shortfall remaining in 2026-27 after mitigation
findings.quote: the delay in these projects as a result of the lengthy procurement processes required under the Procurement Act 2023 have impacted on the expected revenue to be received from the operator in 2025-26 causing an adverse budget position of £65k

findings.headline: Capital programme severely underspent at £37.9m vs £54.8m budget; projects stalled in procurement
findings.detail: The council budgeted £54.8m for capital but only spent £37.9m. Leisure facilities, cremator works, and Greyfriars regeneration are all stalled in procurement processes, delaying £16.9m of planned investment.
findings.matters: Prolonged procurement delays and capital underspend suggest project delivery problems and may defer revenue streams (e.g., from leisure operator). It also indicates execution risk on regeneration plans that may be financing strategy.
findings.figures: £37.9m spent against £54.8m budget; £16.9m underspent
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2025-26 saw a spend of £37.9m against the budget for the year (including items carried forward from 2024-25) of £54.8m... The significant new items in the 2025-26 Capital budget (the leisure facilities, the cremator works, the Greyfriars regeneration project) are progressing through the relevant procurement processes and increased spend is expected once these have concluded and the works get underway.

findings.headline: Service closures and cuts: Blackfriars venue ceased operation, Museum hours reduced
findings.detail: As part of spending review for 2026-27, the council ceased operating Blackfriars venue from May 2026 and reduced Museum opening hours from April 2026. Festivals & Events funding was also reduced.
findings.matters: Service closures indicate the council is in contraction mode and cutting services to residents due to financial pressure, not strategic choice.
findings.figures: Blackfriars ceased May 2026; Museum hours reduced April 2026
findings.quote: The Blackfriars venue ceased to be operated by the Council from May 2026, and the Museum opening hours were reduced from April 2026. There will also be a reduction in the funding of Festivals & Events.

findings.headline: Major £951k variance between Q3 forecast and Q4 outturn shows forecasting unreliability
findings.detail: The council revised its Q3 forecast by £951k downward by year-end. Officers attribute this to budget monitoring only being in place since December with quality and timeliness issues in underlying data.
findings.matters: A £951k variance (33% of the final overspend) between quarters suggests the council cannot reliably predict its financial position, making budget assumptions unreliable.
findings.figures: £951k movement from Q3 forecast to Q4 outturn
findings.quote: The report highlights the movement between quarter 3 and final outturn which is a downward adjustment of £951k. This is a sizable variance but reflects that the budget monitoring had only been in place since December, so when the quarter 3 figures were produced, there were still issues with the quality and timeliness of the data, both of which are slowly improving.

findings.headline: Resources portfolio overspent by £1.612m, driven by commercial property void costs and tenant administration
findings.detail: The Resources portfolio is the worst performer. Commercial property saw £559k adverse variance due to higher service charge costs where tenants vacated, some entering administration. This suggests asset quality issues and non-performing investments.
findings.matters: Commercial property voids and tenant defaults indicate the council's property investments are underperforming and generating unexpected costs rather than income, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Resources portfolio £1.612m overspend; Commercial Property £559k adverse variance
findings.quote: Costs during Q4 have been higher than forecast as a result of the Council continuing to face higher service charge costs than budgeted where tenants have vacated properties, some at short notice due to entering administration.

findings.headline: External Auditors issued Statutory Recommendations in October 2025
findings.detail: The council faced serious enough governance and financial control issues that auditors formally escalated them via statutory recommendations. These led to unexpected additional costs for professional advice and audit fees.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations indicate auditor concerns about financial control and governance. This is a formal escalation above routine management comments and signals control weaknesses.
findings.figures: £204k additional Financial & Corporate overspend related to professional advice and audit fees on these matters
findings.quote: This also reflects the issues raised in the External Auditors Statutory Recommendations issued in October 2025.

findings.headline: Year-end overspend of £1.125m despite £2.845m increase to base budgets
findings.detail: Members approved a permanent increase of £2.845m to base budgets in January 2026 to address identified budget pressures. Despite this, the council still finished the year £1.125m overspent against the revised budget.
findings.matters: The fact that a multi-million pound budget increase failed to prevent overspend suggests either structural demand problems or inability to control spending, both concerning for creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £2.845m budget increase approved; £1.125m year-end overspend recorded
findings.quote: Members approved a permanent increase to base budgets of £2.845m to address the identified budget pressures... The year-end position is a total overspend of £1,125k.

findings.headline: Council received £15.5m emergency government support because reserves fell negative
findings.detail: In 2024-25, overspends pushed the General Fund into a negative position. The council applied for and was approved for Exceptional Financial Support of £15.5m covering 2024/25, 2025/26 and 2026/27. This is emergency funding for a council unable to balance its accounts.
findings.matters: Negative reserves signal insolvency risk and government bailout is a critical red flag for any lender, as it indicates the council cannot manage its finances and has required state intervention.
findings.figures: £15.5m EFS approval for three-year period
findings.quote: the 2024-25 Statement of Accounts were completed and identified a further significant overspend, resulting in the Council's reserves falling into a negative position and leading to the submission of an Exceptional Financial Support application of £15.5m for 2024/25, 2025/26 & 2026/27, which has been approved.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Recommendation Monitoring Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: Council relying on temporary contractors to establish basic property management systems and controls
findings.detail: To address repairs risk rating, management reporting, and periodic venue assessment, the council hired a temporary person on a 6-month contract starting 19 March 2026 who has experience in estate management systems. The council also notes that a new person is being employed to review and implement contractor control procedures. This suggests the council lacked in-house capacity to address basic asset management compliance.
findings.matters: Dependence on temporary contracts to implement basic governance and asset management controls suggests staffing constraints and potential knowledge gaps in property/asset management.
findings.figures: 6-month temporary contract starting 19 March 2026
findings.quote: A temporary person has been employed and starts on the 19th March who has experience in setting up and using the type of estate management systems that we required to report on these items more effectively.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Recommendation Monitoring Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: Multiple audit recommendations on facilities, asset management, and debt controls remain unimplemented past deadlines with no management updates provided to audit committee
findings.detail: The document shows at least eight audit recommendations with implementation dates ranging from August 2024 to April 2026, nearly all marked "No management update received for this audit committee meeting." These cover facilities access controls, repairs risk rating, NNDR credit balance investigations, leaseholder performance monitoring, lease valuations, and debt recovery policy. This pattern suggests systematic delays in implementing audit actions.
findings.matters: Persistent failure to implement or report on audit recommendations indicates weak internal control governance and raises questions about whether audit findings are being taken seriously at operational level.
findings.figures: Approximately 8 recommendations with exceeded or approaching implementation dates
findings.quote: No management update received for this audit committee meeting

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Recommendation Monitoring Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: Planned £3 million in essential building works over the next two years as part of compliance programme
findings.detail: Following a MEND grant audit, the council has committed to a 10-year planned preventative maintenance plan and will spend £3 million on essential building works over the next two years. The council is also instructing full stock condition surveys across its portfolio to create a 10-year planned maintenance schedule for each building.
findings.matters: A significant capital commitment signals either deferred maintenance backlog or condition issues in the council's property portfolio that require funded remediation.
findings.figures: £3 million over next 2 years
findings.quote: Over the next 2 years, a further £3 million will be spent on essential building works and the 10-year planned preventative maintenance plan will be continually reviewed and updated upon completion of the capital expenditure programme or if further works are required.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Recommendation Monitoring Overdue Recommendations
findings.headline: Health and safety audit recommendation from 2019 now significantly overdue with no management update
findings.detail: The council was instructed to clarify building manager responsibilities regarding premises H&S as part of a Limited Assurance audit in October 2023. The original target date was July 2019; it was revised to January 2026. The council's plan to implement this via a Techforge system was paused after a cyber incident due to lack of available resources. No management update has been received since the November 2023 relaunch meeting.
findings.matters: A seven-year-old H&S audit recommendation still unimplemented signals weak follow-through on audit actions and suggests resource or priority constraints affecting core property compliance.
findings.figures: Original target date 01/07/19, revised to 30/01/26
findings.quote: Following the Cyber incident and a lack of available resources, the project of implementing Techforge was paused. Property Services has relaunched the project and meetings have been agreed with Techforge in November 2023 to redesign the project plan.

findings.headline: Auditor issued statutory recommendations on finance team capacity and in-year financial monitoring processes
findings.detail: The auditor recommended urgent review of the finance team to ensure sufficient capacity and capability, a clear timetable for producing future accounts and AGS, and comprehensive review of in-year financial monitoring and reporting to ensure accuracy and support informed decision-making.
findings.matters: Statutory audit recommendations that question the finance team's capacity indicate the council lacks the capability to prepare accurate accounts or maintain effective financial control. This is a governance failure.
findings.figures: Three statutory recommendations issued on 30 October 2025
findings.quote: We recommend that the Council urgently review the Finance team to ensure that there is sufficient capacity and capability to support the breadth of its activities, including the preparation of accurate financial information to support informed decision making and to meet statutory reporting obligations.

findings.headline: Material accounting errors in pension liabilities and financial instruments; prior year figures remain unaudited
findings.detail: The auditor identified significant errors in the 2023/24 draft accounts including pension re-measurement corrections of £8.078m and £60.292m, overstated asset returns of £5.381m, and multiple misstatements in financial instrument disclosures. Prior year 2022/23 comparatives were also subject to disclaimed opinions and remain unaudited.
findings.matters: Large accounting corrections indicate weak financial reporting quality and increase the risk that material misstatement remains undetected. Unaudited prior years prevent reliable year-on-year comparison.
findings.figures: Pension error corrections: £8.078m (business combinations disposal), £60.292m (asset ceiling), £5.381m (return on assets overstated); pension re-measurement correction £8.078m
findings.quote: The CIES table includes a number of errors, specifically: The inclusion of the effect of business combinations and disposals of £8.078 million, which has been incorrectly presented; An asset ceiling adjustment of £-60.292 million has been incorrectly included

findings.headline: Council depleted all usable reserves and entered negative general fund reserve position; now dependent on government emergency funding
findings.detail: The council overspent its 2023/24 budget by £0.826 million (vs £0.288m initially reported), reducing reserves from £4.975m to £3.099m. In December 2025, council identified £4.3m overspend for 2024/25, resulting in negative general fund reserves of £3.89m. Unable to set balanced budget for 2025/26, council applied for and received Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) of £15.5 million in-principle from government.
findings.matters: A negative reserve position indicates the council cannot absorb unexpected costs or service demands. Dependency on emergency government funding signals financial distress and indicates the council cannot manage its finances sustainably.
findings.figures: 2023/24 overspend £0.826m; 2024/25 overspend £4.3m; negative reserves position £3.89m; EFS received £15.5m in-principle
findings.quote: In December 2025, the Council identified overspends of £4.3 million against the 2024/25 budget and a forecast overspend of £2.5 million against the 2025/26 budget. This resulted in the Council being in a negative general fund reserve position of £3.89 million for 2024/25.

findings.headline: Council lacks fundamental internal control framework: monthly reconciliations and budget monitoring not operating effectively
findings.detail: The council did not complete monthly control account reconciliations (including bank reconciliations) or maintain robust budget monitoring processes during 2023/24. The Council also operated hybrid manual and system-based records from March 2023 to April 2024 following the December 2021 cyber-attack, which the auditor identified as a significant risk of misstatement.
findings.matters: Absence of basic financial controls increases the risk of error, fraud, and misstatement in financial reporting. It limits oversight of resource use and the council's ability to manage its finances responsibly.
findings.figures: Manual records maintained 20 December 2021 to 28 February 2023; hybrid processes 1 March 2023 to 18 April 2024
findings.quote: The Council did not have an appropriate internal control framework to ensure that fundamental controls, such as: the completion of monthly control account reconciliations; the preparation of monthly bank reconciliations: and robust budget monitoring processes were operating effectively during 2023/24.

findings.headline: Auditor will issue a disclaimed audit opinion on the 2023/24 financial statements, meaning no assurance over the accounts
findings.detail: The auditor could not complete the necessary audit procedures due to the 28 February 2025 backstop date and delays in receiving draft accounts (published 8 September 2025, 16 months late). Combined with prior year disclaimers, this means no assurance over opening balances, in-year transactions, or closing balances.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the council's financial position is unaudited and unverified. Lenders and finance directors cannot rely on the accounts for decision-making.
findings.figures: Backstop date 28 February 2025; accounts published 8 September 2025, 16 months after statutory deadline of 31 May 2024
findings.quote: for the year ended 31 March 2024 we determined that we cannot meet the objectives of the ISAs(UK) and we anticipate issuing a disclaimed audit report.

findings.headline: Original governance statement revised following recent financial position concerns identified by auditors
findings.detail: The original AGS approved in July 2024 was updated after internal finance raised financial position concerns that featured in External Auditors Statutory Recommendations. The Head of Internal Audit and Section 151 Officer worked with external auditors on the revised final statement, which has been reviewed and amended.
findings.matters: External Auditor Statutory Recommendations signalling financial position concerns warrant formal revision of governance — indicates material issues requiring management attention and audit oversight
findings.quote: To provide a final AGS following the recent financial position highlighted by the internal finance team and included in the External Auditors Statutory Recommendations. This has been reviewed by the External Auditors and amendments are included.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing by £12.077m; net borrowing of £15.024m required in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's cumulative debt (CFR) will increase by £12.077m during 2026/27 to reach £285.993m. Of the £22.603m capital programme, £15.024m will be financed through net borrowing (66% of total expenditure), with the remainder met from external grants (£4.169m), capital receipts (£1.2m), and revenue funding (£2.21m). This reliance on borrowing compounds existing high financing costs.
findings.matters: A lender tracks debt accumulation and borrowing requirements. The substantial CFR growth and high proportion of debt financing show the council is taking on material new debt commitments that will extend debt service obligations for decades, combining with existing revenue constraints.
findings.figures: CFR increase £12.077m, total CFR £285.993m, net financing need £15.024m, borrowing 66% of capital expenditure
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £12.077m during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Financing costs consume 37% of net revenue, indicating material debt burden and constrained financial flexibility
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs (interest and minimum revenue provision on debt) to net revenue stream stands at 37.17% in 2026/27, remaining at 37.27% in 2027/28 and 37.20% in 2028/29. This means over one-third of the council's available revenue is committed to debt service before any spending on services, significantly limiting the council's ability to respond to unexpected financial pressures or fund new initiatives.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness must understand the council's revenue flexibility and debt burden. A financing costs ratio of 37% is materially high and indicates the council is heavily committed to historical borrowing decisions, constraining its capacity to absorb financial shocks.
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream 37.17%

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Reserve levels inadequate and forecast to go negative without recovery plan delivery
findings.detail: The council's minimum prudent reserve level is determined to be £1.3m. Earmarked reserves at 31 March 2027 are estimated at £1.962m, but the forecast shows general fund balance going negative in 2027/28 (£1,603m deficit), 2028/29 (£3,264m deficit) and 2029/30 (£3,857m deficit) without delivery of the recovery plan and further EFS.
findings.matters: Negative reserves indicate insolvency. The council cannot sustain operations without continued government support or dramatic operational changes.
findings.figures: Minimum prudent reserves £1.3m; forecast 2027/28 general fund balance minus £1,603m; 2028/29 minus £3,264m; 2029/30 minus £3,857m
findings.quote: the forecast of usable unrestricted Earmarked Revenue Reserves and the General Fund balance over the period 2025/26 to 2030/31...demonstrates that the Council is not financially sustainable in the medium term

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Recovery plan and governance arrangements still under development and not yet approved
findings.detail: The EFS approval is conditional on delivering a recovery plan including asset disposals and £1m+ in savings/income improvements. However, governance arrangements for the recovery plan were still awaiting approval at the time of this report. The Council set up a 'Recovery Command and Control' group using emergency planning protocols, treating the situation as if a Section 114 Notice had been issued.
findings.matters: Conditions on government support have not yet been operationalised. Failure to establish effective governance risks non-delivery and triggering further intervention.
findings.figures: Recovery plan requires £1m savings/income 2026/27, further £1m for 2027/28; £15.5m EFS conditional on recovery plan delivery
findings.quote: Governance arrangements for delivery of the Council's Recovery Plan needs to be approved to ensure this can be demonstrated to the MHCLG now EFS has been approved

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Forced service closures and reductions to fund deficit
findings.detail: The council is ceasing operation of Blackfriars Priory from May 2026, reducing museum opening hours from 6 to 4 days, cutting festivals and events support, reducing staffing, and changing community safety management. These are described as part of 'review of Council's discretionary spend' totalling £377k in savings.
findings.matters: Service cuts indicate the scale of fiscal pressure and reduced capacity to respond to new demands or invest in service improvements.
findings.figures: £377k savings from service reductions; total recovery plan requires £1m savings in 2026/27 and further £1m in 2027/28
findings.quote: Cease to operate Blackfriars Priory from May 2026; Keep the Museum of Gloucester Open but reduce its opening hours from April 2026 from 6 to 4 days

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: External auditors issued three statutory recommendations on finance capacity, accounting timeliness, and monitoring
findings.detail: In October 2025, Ernst & Young issued statutory recommendations under Section 24 of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 requiring: urgent review of Finance team capacity and capability; clear timetable for producing accounts (the council failed to meet statutory deadlines); and comprehensive review of in-year financial monitoring. The recommendations were presented to Full Council on 25 November 2025.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations indicate external auditor concerns about control environment and financial governance. This creates risk of audit qualification and potential government intervention.
findings.figures: Three statutory recommendations issued October 2025; council accounts production delayed beyond statutory deadlines
findings.quote: We recommend that the Council urgently review the Finance team to ensure that there is sufficient capacity and capability to support the breadth of its activities, including the preparation of accurate financial information

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Commercial property income and bereavement services significantly underperforming budget
findings.detail: Commercial property budgets had to be reduced by £1.777m in mid-year (from £3.317m budgeted to £1.540m actual), indicating serious income shortfalls. Bereavement services are also flagged as an ongoing budgetary challenge. These are identified in the financial monitoring report as key drivers of the £2.5m projected overspend.
findings.matters: Income shortfalls on assets indicate either market challenges in the council's area or asset management issues. This affects debt serviceability.
findings.figures: Commercial property adverse variance £1,777k; combined income service pressures a key factor in £2.5m 2025/26 overspend
findings.quote: ongoing budgetary challenges for the Council's commercial properties income, bereavement services income, IT spending, waste spending, and housing subsidy budgets

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Pattern of serious annual overspends indicating systemic budget management failure
findings.detail: The council has overspent significantly for multiple consecutive years: 2022/23 (£725k), 2023/24 (£826k), 2024/25 (£4.3m), and 2025/26 (forecast £2.5m). In 2025/26, budgets had to be revised mid-year adding £2.845m to the net budget because budgets were set at 'unrealistic levels'. The Section 151 Officer cites 'lack of financial data, lack of engagement with budget officers and limited budget monitoring' as causes.
findings.matters: This demonstrates systemic failure in financial controls, not one-off issues. External auditors issued three statutory recommendations specifically addressing capacity, monitoring, and accounts production.
findings.figures: 2025/26 mid-year budget revision added £2,845k; year-end forecast overspend £2.519m; commercial property had £1,777k adverse variance from budget
findings.quote: some key service budgets were set at unrealistic levels for a number of years through a combination of lack of financial data, lack of engagement with budget officers and limited budget monitoring

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: High short-term borrowing exposure to interest rate risk of approximately £122m
findings.detail: The council has a significant amount of short-term borrowing estimated at around £122m, which creates high sensitivity to interest rate changes. The Section 151 Officer notes that base rates reducing slower than expected has already had direct negative impact. The strategy going forward is to work with treasury advisors to mitigate this risk 'if affordable', suggesting limited capacity to refinance.
findings.matters: Even small interest rate movements could materially worsen the council's revenue position. This is identified as an active risk that may not be manageable given budget pressures.
findings.figures: Approximately £122m short-term borrowing; Bank of England base rate 3.75% in December 2025
findings.quote: A significant amount of the Council s borrowing approximately £122m is short term which leaves a high risk of exposure to interest rate changes

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget entirely dependent on one-off government support with no sustainable funding plan for 2027/28
findings.detail: The £9.050m EFS for 2026/27 is a one-off capitalisation direction that 'defers the budget pressure into 2027/28'. The council forecasts deficits of £4.3m in 2027/28 and general fund balances going negative from 2028/29 onwards. The Section 151 Officer states the council 'is currently unable to demonstrate Financial Sustainability over the medium term' and that 'further EFS will be required in 2027/28' if the recovery plan is not delivered.
findings.matters: The council faces a structural funding gap that extends beyond the current support package. Future borrowing capacity and creditworthiness are at serious risk.
findings.figures: 2027/28 deficit forecast £4,316k; 2028/29 negative balance of £2,905m; 2029/30 negative balance of £3,857m
findings.quote: The Council is currently unable to demonstrate Financial Sustainability over the medium term. If this is not delivered it is likely that further EFS will be required in 2027/28

findings.paper_title: Money Plan 2026-31 & Budget Proposals 2026-27 (Revised Appendix B)
findings.headline: Council received emergency government funding to avoid insolvency notice
findings.detail: Gloucester was in a Section 114 position (negative reserves) in 2024/25 with a £4.3m overspend. The council applied for Exceptional Financial Support in December 2025 and received approval on 23 February 2026 for a £15.5m capitalisation direction spanning three years. Without this, the council would have been unable to set a lawful budget and would have been required to issue a Section 114 Notice.
findings.matters: This is a direct indicator of severe financial distress. The council was technically insolvent and dependent on government bailout to function.
findings.quote: without EFS this Council would have been in Section 114

findings.headline: Previous years' overspends and budget resets indicate historical budget management failures
findings.detail: The council acknowledges it is 'facing significant financial pressures due to previous years overspends' and the current plan 'includes the financial impact of the previous year's overspends, the budget reset in 25-26'. This is not a one-off pressure from external events but a pattern: the council's budgets have been wrong for multiple years. The 2025/26 opening balance is stated as zero (adjusted for a £3.89m EFS contribution), indicating the council was cash-generative only through emergency support.
findings.matters: Historical budget mismanagement is a warning sign for future reliability. If a council has consistently overspent its budget for multiple years, that suggests either forecasting is poor or spending control is weak. The current 'balanced' budget achieved only through emergency support and asset disposals inherits this risk.
findings.figures: 2025/26 opening balance: £0 (adjusted from negative position with £3.89m EFS contribution to General Fund balances); 2025/26 budget deficit before EFS: £2.270m
findings.quote: The Council is facing significant financial pressures due to previous years overspends. It explains what the Council is doing to address those pressures and achieve a sustainable medium-term budget including by delivering the initiatives/actions detailed in the recovery plan.

findings.headline: Council identifies lack of finance and property team capacity as critical constraint on recovery plan delivery
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly states that 'sufficient capacity needs to be in place for the Council's finance and property teams' to deliver the recovery plan, and this is conditional language: the budget is only 'robust' if this condition is met. The council's own risk assessment identifies 'Finance Team and Asset Management Team capacity and capability' as a risk, with no residual risk score provided (suggesting it may be unmitigated). This suggests the council is already stretched and cannot reliably execute the asset disposal plan or other recovery initiatives.
findings.matters: Even if the council has a good plan on paper, its ability to execute complex asset disposals and service reductions depends on having adequate staff. Understaffed finance teams make implementation errors, miss deadlines, and slow delivery. This is a deliverability constraint.
findings.figures: Recovery plan and budget robustness conditional on adequate finance and property team capacity; Finance/Asset Management team capacity identified as risk factor in 19.3
findings.quote: To deliver the plan, sufficient capacity needs to be in place for the Council's finance and property teams, and governance arrangements need to robust and clear.

findings.headline: £1.297m annual revenue cost for EFS borrowing built into budget indefinitely
findings.detail: The council must service the £15.5m EFS as revenue borrowing, with costs of £1,297k per year shown consistently across all five years of the plan (2026/27 through 2030/31). This is a structural revenue cost that does not diminish. If the recovery plan asset disposal targets are not met, this borrowing persists and consumes revenue funding that could otherwise fund services or be returned to reserves.
findings.matters: This represents a permanent structural claim on revenue: over the five-year plan, £6.485m will be spent servicing this one emergency loan. The council is paying interest on money it couldn't afford in the first place.
findings.quote: Cost of EFS Borrowing 1,297 [per year]. A Capitalisation Direction is funded by the Council borrowing or use of Capital Receipts (e.g. from disposal of assets) which makes delivery of the recovery plan essential

findings.headline: Negative fund balances forecast from 2027/28 onwards, extending through the five-year plan
findings.detail: Despite EFS approval, the General Fund balance turns negative from 2027/28 (£-1,603k) and deteriorates further to £-4,311k by 2030/31. The council explicitly states 'The Money Plan presents negative balances from 2027/28' and acknowledges this 'indicates that the current recovery plan will require phase two initiatives to achieve further reductions to the base budget.' This shows the council's own financial projections indicate the recovery plan will not be sufficient to stabilise finances.
findings.matters: Negative reserves mean the council is operating at a structural loss. Each year it runs a cash deficit that must be covered by reserves or further borrowing. This is unsustainable and suggests the council will run out of cash.
findings.quote: The Money Plan presents negative balances from 2027/28, but this includes the borrowing costs for the £15.5m from 1 April 2026. The draft recovery plan submitted as part of the EFS application sets out an Asset Disposal Plan, generating sufficient capital receipts which, if EFS is granted, may be used to temporarily support the cost of revenue spending

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balanced only through £15.5m exceptional government support, conditional on recovery plan delivery
findings.detail: The council cannot set a balanced budget without in-principle Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from MHCLG for a capitalisation directive of up to £15.5m. The Section 151 Officer confirms that this sum is 'required to enable a legally, robust and Balanced Budget to be set and to avoid a Section 151 notice being required in relation to 2026/27'. The budget is contingent on MHCLG acceptance of terms and delivery of the recovery plan.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot balance its budget from its own resources and is entirely dependent on government emergency support. A Section 151 notice would be a formal statement that the council cannot set a balanced budget.
findings.figures: £15.5m capitalisation directive covering 2024/25, 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.quote: a balanced budget for 2026-27 was only achievable due to the in principle agreement by the MHCLG for Exceptional Financial Support for a capitalisation directive of up to £15.5m

findings.headline: Ongoing impact of December 2021 cyber-attack rendered council unable to demonstrate ability to monitor deployment of resources
findings.detail: The 2021 cyber-attack disabled the council's financial systems from December 2021 to February 2023, during which the council maintained only manual records. From March 2023 to April 2024 a hybrid manual-and-system process was used. Throughout this period and beyond, the council was unable to demonstrate the ability to appropriately monitor the deployment of its resources in pursuit of its objectives.
findings.matters: Inability to monitor resource deployment for extended periods is a critical governance and control failure that enabled financial problems to go undetected.
findings.figures: Systems down December 2021 to February 2023; hybrid process March 2023 to April 2024
findings.quote: the attack rendered the Council's financial systems unavailable from 20 December 2021 to 28 February 2023, after which the Council operated a hybrid manual-and-system process from 1 March 2023 to 18 April 2024. During and following this period the Council has been significantly impacted with its servers rendering the Council's system inaccessible as a consequence, the Council was unable to demonstrate the ability to appropriately monitor the deployment of its resources in pursuit of its objectives.

findings.headline: Annual Governance Statement does not disclose known significant weaknesses in financial reporting and internal controls
findings.detail: The council's draft 2023/24 Annual Governance Statement (AGS) does not reflect known significant weaknesses in financial reporting or internal control arrangements. Management and the Audit Committee failed to consider or disclose the implications of identified key control failures, including that bank reconciliations were not up to date and internal audit had to defer reviews.
findings.matters: When a council fails to disclose known control weaknesses in its governance statement, it misleads stakeholders about the reliability of its financial management and loses transparency.
findings.figures: Known weaknesses in control environment not disclosed in AGS
findings.quote: The Council's draft 2023/24 AGS does not reflect the known significant weaknesses in financial reporting or internal control arrangements. In preparing and considering the AGS management and the Audit and Governance Committee should have considered implications of the fact that Internal Audit identified that key control account reconciliations, including bank reconciliations were not up to date

findings.headline: Finance team lacks sufficient capacity and capability to prepare financial statements to required standard and timetable
findings.detail: The council has a recent history of late financial statements (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25 all late). The core cause is insufficient capacity and capability within the finance team. This chronic weakness has prevented timely, accurate financial reporting and has contributed to control failures and misstatements in the accounts.
findings.matters: Without adequate finance team capacity and capability, councils cannot produce timely, accurate financial information needed for statutory reporting, audit, and informed decision-making.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years of late accounts (2021/22 through 2024/25); 16 months late for 2023/24
findings.quote: The Council has a recent history of not preparing its financial statements in accordance with the statutory publication deadlines with 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts being late. This is primarily due to insufficient capacity and capability within the finance team

findings.headline: 2023/24 internal audit plan, as directed by management, failed to adequately cover key financial system risks
findings.detail: Management directed internal audit to defer reviews of areas with known control risks. As a result, fundamental weaknesses in the internal control framework were not identified or reported. Internal audit did not provide the assurance over financial controls that it should have.
findings.matters: When management restricts internal audit scope to avoid detection of known weaknesses, the council loses its primary internal safeguard against financial and governance failures.
findings.figures: Multiple audit areas deferred due to data recovery issues
findings.quote: the 2023/24 Internal Audit plan which Management directed did not adequately ensure there was appropriate coverage of key financial system risks at the Council. Management instructed internal audit to defer their review of these areas

findings.headline: Council did not operate fundamental internal controls including monthly bank reconciliations and control account reconciliations during 2023/24
findings.detail: Critical financial controls were absent: monthly bank reconciliations and control account reconciliations were not completed during 2023/24. The responsible Section 151 Officer did not fully discharge their responsibility to maintain an effective system of internal controls. This was partly a legacy of the 2021 cyber-attack but also represents a governance failure to restore these controls.
findings.matters: Absence of basic reconciliation controls creates high risk of undetected error and fraud, and indicates breakdown in financial oversight fundamental to any creditworthy organisation.
findings.figures: No monthly bank reconciliations; no monthly control account reconciliations during 2023/24
findings.quote: the Council did not operate a number of fundamental internal controls during 2023/24 including monthly control account reconciliations and the preparation of monthly bank reconciliations

findings.headline: Effective budget monitoring controls did not exist in 2023/24, preventing timely identification of emerging overspends
findings.detail: The council had no effective budget monitoring processes in place, meaning areas of overspend were not identified in a timely manner. This lack of control prevented the council from promptly identifying, challenging and responding to emerging financial pressures. The underlying 2023/24 budget was also based on incorrect assumptions that were rolled forward without updating.
findings.matters: Without effective budget monitoring, councils cannot manage resources responsibly or detect financial problems early enough to implement mitigating action, leading to larger deficits.
findings.figures: Budget set on incorrect assumptions; £0.826 million actual overspend not caught until accounts closure
findings.quote: the Council did not have in place effective budget monitoring processes, to enable it to identify areas of overspend in a timely basis thereby adversely limiting its ability to identify, challenge, and respond to emerging financial pressures with the implementation of appropriate mitigating action in a timely manner.

findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinions issued for 2023/24 and anticipated for 2024/25 due to late financial statement publication
findings.detail: A disclaimed opinion was issued on 27 January 2025 for 2023/24 accounts due to delayed publication (16 months late). The 2024/25 accounts have still not been published at the date of this February 2026 report, making a disclaimed opinion inevitable for that year too. This means the auditors cannot provide assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatement.
findings.matters: Disclaimed audit opinions eliminate auditor assurance and are a severe governance red flag indicating financial reporting breakdowns that prevent effective accountability and decision-making.
findings.figures: 2023/24 accounts published 8 September 2025 (statutory date was 31 May 2024, 16 months late); 2024/25 accounts still unpublished as of February 2026
findings.quote: The Council published the draft unaudited financial statements on 8 September 2025, sixteen months after the statutory publication date of 31 May 2024. We were therefore not in a position to undertake any audit procedures or to start rebuilding assurance ahead of the backstop date of 28 February 2025.

findings.headline: Council has negative general fund reserves of £3.89 million and applied for emergency government funding
findings.detail: After overspending £0.826 million in 2023/24, reserves fell from £4.975 million to £3.099 million. Overspends of £4.3 million in 2024/25 and forecast £2.5 million in 2025/26 have left the council unable to set a balanced budget. The council has applied for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from government to bridge funding gaps while establishing cost reduction and income increase plans.
findings.matters: A council with negative reserves and requiring emergency government funding is an extreme credit risk for lenders and indicates fundamental financial instability.
findings.figures: £3.89 million negative reserves for 2024/25; £4.3 million overspend 2024/25; £2.5 million forecast overspend 2025/26; £0.826 million overspend 2023/24
findings.quote: the Council is unable to set a balanced budget and has applied for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from the Government to address the budget gaps which it faces while it establishes plans to achieve reductions in expenditure and increases income in order to balance the Council's financial position

findings.headline: Cemeteries and Crematorium service income underperforming by £496k due to structural decline
findings.detail: Income from cremations and related services has declined because of a trend towards direct cremations rather than full cremations, reducing wake bookings. This is a structural demand change, not temporary.
findings.matters: A £496k structural revenue loss from changed consumer behaviour indicates permanently reduced capacity in this income stream.
findings.figures: £496k shortfall in income
findings.quote: Cemeteries and Crematorium service income is underperforming to budget by £496k. This trend has been clear over a few years in part due to more direct cremations to be taking place, which is leading to a resultant reduction in the demand for full cremations.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio income down by £1.8m
findings.detail: The council's commercial property income is now forecast at £1.5m net, a reduction of £1.8m. Much of the estate is retail-based and affected by city centre regeneration completion and historic portfolio recovery slowness.
findings.matters: Commercial property is a significant income source; the £1.8m reduction and regeneration completion risk create revenue volatility that could affect debt service capacity.
findings.figures: £1.5m forecast income; £1.8m reduction from budget
findings.quote: Commercial Property portfolio is now forecast to contribute a net income to the Council of over £1.5m, a reduction of £1.8m.

findings.headline: £2.8m budget increase in 2025-26 due to unrealistic baseline budgets set for years
findings.detail: Service budgets have been set at unrealistic levels for years due to lack of financial data, poor engagement between finance and budget holders, and limited budget monitoring. This is why the revised budget requires a £2.8m increase.
findings.matters: This reveals systemic budget-setting failures that explain prior overspends and indicate ongoing budget volatility risk; budgets still may not reflect true costs.
findings.figures: £2.8m (£2.845m) increase in net budget requirement
findings.quote: some key service budgets have been set at unrealistic levels for a number of years through a combination of lack of financial data, lack of engagement between finance team and budget holding officers and limited budget monitoring

findings.headline: Council has failed to publish statutory accounts on time for four years
findings.detail: Since the December 2021 cyber attack, the council has not met statutory deadlines for publishing Annual Statements of Accounts. Accounts for 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24 were eventually published in late 2024 and 2025.
findings.matters: Failure to publish accounts on time indicates governance breakdown and prevents creditors, auditors, and lenders from understanding the council's true financial position in a timely way.
findings.figures: 4 years of missed deadlines; accounts for 2021-22, 2022-23, 2023-24 eventually published
findings.quote: This Council has not met the statutory deadlines for publishing its Annual Statement of Accounts since the cyber attack in December 2021.

findings.headline: External auditors issued Statutory Recommendations notice in October 2025
findings.detail: This formal notice was issued by external auditors and approved by Council in November 2025. It indicates governance and financial control failures serious enough to warrant statutory intervention.
findings.matters: Statutory Recommendations indicate formal audit concerns about the council's governance and financial management; they typically precede more severe intervention if not addressed.
findings.figures: October 2025
findings.quote: In October 2025 the External Auditors issued a Statutory Recommendations notice; these, along with the Council's response, were approved by Members unanimously at Council on 25th November.

findings.headline: 2026-27 budget can only be delivered with Exceptional Financial Support from government
findings.detail: The council has explicitly stated it cannot balance its 2026-27 budget without EFS. This dependency will continue into the forward plan and indicates the council cannot sustain itself on its own revenues.
findings.matters: Dependency on government bailout is the strongest signal of financial distress; lenders cannot rely on repayment without explicit central guarantee.
findings.figures: 2026-27 budget undeliverable without EFS
findings.quote: the 2026-27 budget can only be delivered with EFS

findings.headline: General fund reserves are in negative balance
findings.detail: The council's 2024-25 draft accounts show an overspend of £4.3m that pushed general fund reserves into negative territory. This represents a fundamental breach of prudent financial reserves policy and indicates the council cannot meet unexpected demands without external support.
findings.matters: Negative reserves mean the council is technically insolvent and unable to manage financial volatility—a critical risk for lenders assessing repayment capacity.
findings.figures: £4.3m overspend; negative general fund reserves
findings.quote: This level of overspend took the general fund reserves into a negative position.

findings.paper_title: Kings Quarter Phase 2 - KQ Hotel Management Company No2 Ltd Mobilisation Loan Agreement
findings.headline: Council is capturing a £982k spread by borrowing at 5.54% and lending at 7.25%, betting on sustained operational performance
findings.detail: The council borrows from PWLB at 5.54%, lends to the hotel management company at 3.5% over base rate (currently 7.25%), and expects to net £982,207 in interest return over 20 years. This spread depends on the hotel management company being able to service its loan obligations — if performance falters, this return is at risk.
findings.matters: The council is treating this as a financial asset generating return, but the return is contingent on a trading business succeeding. In a downturn, the council would be carrying the debt cost whilst losing the expected return.
findings.figures: PWLB rate 5.54%; hotel company rate 7.25% (3.5% over base); expected net interest return of £3.698m less £2.717m = £982,207 over 20 years
findings.quote: The differential between the Council's borrowing cost and the loan extended to the Management Company is £982,207, which is an additional return to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Kings Quarter Phase 2 - KQ Hotel Management Company No2 Ltd Mobilisation Loan Agreement
findings.headline: Expected rental income and dividend distributions are deferred to 2027/28 or later, creating early cash flow gap
findings.detail: The lease includes a two-year rent-free period expiring in 2026, followed by an additional one-year rent-free period, meaning base rent of £500k per annum does not commence until 2027/28. Dividend distributions are expected only after loan obligations are discharged and the management company demonstrates financial stability — not anticipated before 2027/28.
findings.matters: The council is borrowing now but will not receive rent or dividend income for over 18 months. If the hotel's operations are weaker than forecast, the council will be carrying this risk and carrying costs with no offsetting revenue.
findings.figures: £500k per annum base rent from 2027/28; no rent payments expected until then
findings.quote: the first rent instalments scheduled to commence in the 2027/28 financial year, in line with the Commercial Revenue Plan. Dividend payments to the City Council will only commence once loan obligations have been fully discharged and the Management Company demonstrates sustained financial stability. These provisions are expected to deliver a consistent medium- to long-term income stream

findings.paper_title: Kings Quarter Phase 2 - KQ Hotel Management Company No2 Ltd Mobilisation Loan Agreement
findings.headline: Council bears ultimate responsibility for hotel's commercial success and must take over operations if management company fails
findings.detail: The council retains ownership of the asset and assumes trading risk. If the management company fails, the lease reverts to the council, which would then be forced to directly employ all staff and manage operational matters with IHG. This creates an open-ended contingent liability on the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: This is material unquantified operational and financial risk. If the hotel does not trade profitably, the council cannot step back — it must either absorb losses directly or find capital to close the operation, both of which could worsen an already stretched financial position.
findings.figures: £4 million loan; hotel is expected to employ over 60 staff directly
findings.quote: Gloucester City Council bears ultimate responsibility for the commercial success of the hotel as per The Forum Phase 2 Cabinet report 15 June 2022. Financial failure of the KQ Hotel management company could result in the Lease reverting to the Council who would then have to directly employ all the staff and become involved in assisting IHG Hotel group for operational matters.

findings.paper_title: Kings Quarter Phase 2 - KQ Hotel Management Company No2 Ltd Mobilisation Loan Agreement
findings.headline: Council is borrowing whilst in Exceptional Financial Support due to negative reserves
findings.detail: The council reported in December that it has sought Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to address negative reserves and current financial challenges. Despite this position, it is now approving a £4 million borrowing from PWLB at 5.54% to fund the hotel loan. The council states this borrowing requirement was part of the original business plan and does not impede PWLB eligibility, but the timing — whilst in EFS — is material context.
findings.matters: A council in financial difficulty taking on new borrowing and trading risk is a significant consideration for lenders assessing creditworthiness, and suggests the council is dependent on this development's success to restore financial position.
findings.figures: £4 million borrowing at 5.54% from PWLB; total repayment obligation of £6,716,580 over 20 years
findings.quote: As reported in December the Council has sought Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to address its current financial challenges and negative reserves position; however, this does not impede its ability to access borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB).

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: Multi-track cost-cutting programme includes restructuring, asset monetisation, and service reductions
findings.detail: Council pursuing parallel cuts across recruitment (reviewing temporary positions, suspending apprenticeships), fees and charges increases, non-essential spend review, operational restructuring (including review of Ubico waste contract scope and housing revenue reduction), and commissioned Asset Management Review to extract higher income from asset portfolio. Car park charges increased from November 2025.
findings.matters: The breadth and simultaneous launch of these initiatives signals material financial distress; asset monetisation and service reduction typically indicate a council under urgent financial pressure.
findings.figures: Car park charges increased from November 2025; multiple workstreams with no specific targets disclosed
findings.quote: Officers are exploring further restructuring options and other operational efficiencies (including the scope of the Ubico contract and further capital actions to reduce housing revenue spend) and income generation opportunities. Officers have commissioned an Asset Management Review to develop a higher income generating profile from its Asset Portfolio.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: Budget monitoring processes have been 'not consistent and robust since the cyber attack'
findings.detail: Collaborative budget monitoring between finance and budget officers collapsed after cyber attack and remains inadequate. Council appointed interim accountant for three months to rebuild processes. Finance officers now assigned to specific cost centres. Monthly budget monitoring process rolling out starting November figures. Budget monitoring is now standing monthly agenda item.
findings.matters: Weak in-year monitoring means budget variances are not caught promptly; given zero budget slack, any overspend cannot be absorbed and forces mid-year cuts.
findings.figures: Interim accountant for three-month period; rollout planned for November 2025 figures
findings.quote: Collaborative budget monitoring with the Budget officers has not been consistent and robust since the cyber attack, an additional Accountant has been appointed for three months to set up a budget monitoring process that engages with budget officers and Portfolio Holders

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: Finance team capacity and capability insufficient; formal auditor recommendation for urgent structural review
findings.detail: Auditor formally recommends urgent review of finance team structure and capability. Team was forced onto spreadsheet systems during cyber attack recovery and has not recovered full capacity. Council commissioned Local Government Association structural review (commencing 24 November, results due January 2026) and appointed interim accountant for three months to rebuild core processes.
findings.matters: Finance team weakness directly causes missed deadlines and broken budget control; understaffing or under-skilled teams correlate with further financial deterioration.
findings.figures: New Section 151 Officer commenced April 2025; LGA review to commence 24 November 2025; outcomes January 2026; interim accountant for three months
findings.quote: We recommend that the Council urgently review the Finance team to ensure that there is sufficient capacity and capability to support the breadth of its activities, including the preparation of accurate financial information to support informed decision making and to meet statutory reporting obligations.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: General fund reserves depleted to critical level by multi-year overspends with no buffer for 2026-27 budget
findings.detail: Overspends in 2022-23, 2023-24, and estimated 2024-25 have reduced reserves by £1.5m. Cabinet told in September 2025 that without urgent expenditure cuts and income increases, the council will struggle to deliver a balanced 2026-27 budget. Budget monitoring summary states 'there is no margin for variances' in the coming year.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves eliminate financial flexibility and indicate deteriorating sustainability; a council unable to balance budget without cuts is a material credit risk for lenders.
findings.figures: £1.5m reduction in reserves from overspends across 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25
findings.quote: The estimated impact at this time was a reduction of £1.5m and it was made clear in this report without urgent actions to reduce expenditure and increase income to increase reserves next years budget would be challenging to deliver.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors Ernst & Young – Statutory Recommendations (Report)
findings.headline: Annual accounts publication deadlines missed every year since December 2021 cyber attack
findings.detail: The council has failed to meet statutory account publication deadlines for four consecutive years following a cyber attack that destroyed the finance IT system. 2021-22 accounts published February 2024 (14 months late); 2022-23 published 27 January 2025 (also substantially late). The council faces a 27 February 2026 backstop to deliver 2023-24 audited accounts.
findings.matters: Delayed accounts prevent timely financial transparency to council members and lenders; this pattern over four years suggests systematic finance function failure, not a temporary recovery issue.
findings.figures: Cyber attack December 2021; 2021-22 published February 2024; 2022-23 published 27 January 2025; 27 February 2026 backstop for 2023-24
findings.quote: This Council has not met the statutory deadlines for publishing its Annual Statement of Accounts since the cyber attack in December 2021.

findings.headline: Council borrowing short-term to fund Forum development with refinancing decision deferred until project completion
findings.detail: Gloucester chose to fund the Forum development with short-term borrowing rather than long-term PWLB borrowing. The council acknowledges the Forum is still under construction and will make a decision on permanent funding structure once the asset is complete, meaning the borrowing will be refinanced at that future point.
findings.matters: Capital project funding arrangements matter to lenders. Using short-term borrowing for a long-term asset creates refinancing risk: if rates rise before the project is finished, the eventual refinancing cost will exceed the current short-term costs.
findings.figures: Bank Rate reduced from 5.25% to 4.50% during 2024/25; short-term investment returns averaged 3.70%
findings.quote: The council have taken the decision to borrow short term to fund the Forum development, short-term rates are lower than long term due to the Normal Guilt curve we are experiencing. Once the asset is complete we will make a decision, alongside our advisors, on the best way to structure our borrowing.

findings.headline: £80m property investment fund established with governance safeguards against political interference in commercial decisions
findings.detail: Gloucester has created a Property Investment Board to oversee an £80m property investment fund. The board evaluates acquisitions, makes recommendations to the s151 Officer, and oversees due diligence in accordance with the Property Investment Strategy. The council has delegated authority to the Council Solicitor to conclude transaction documents. The identified risk is that political priorities could dilute commercial considerations around the investment.
findings.matters: £80m represents material borrowing and investment; lenders track how councils govern major capital programmes and whether governance structures can insulate commercial decisions from political pressure
findings.figures: £80m fund
findings.quote: Property Investment Board set up with a defined Terms of Reference to oversee the investment of the £80m fund.

findings.headline: Cyber incident recovery requiring significant capital investment in IT rebuild and security infrastructure
findings.detail: Gloucester experienced a cyber incident and has rebuilt its IT infrastructure in partnership with NCSC and NCC. The council has invested in additional security products including SIEM, endpoint protection, email scanning, and physical security controls, and is accelerating a cloud-first strategy. An investment budget to implement and maintain the rebuild has been approved.
findings.matters: Major cyber incidents represent material operational and governance risk; recovery costs and ongoing security investment affect capital plans and operational resilience
findings.figures: Investment budget approved (specific amount not stated in register)
findings.quote: The rebuild opportunity following the cyber incident has enabled the council to accelerate its cloud first strategy. The investment budget to implement and maintain the rebuild has been agreed

news_drafts.headline: Capital programme is 36% underspent overall at mid-year
news_drafts.lead: Significant capital programme slippage indicates the council may not deliver planned investment, requiring reforecasting and affecting growth and regeneration plans that support financial sustainability

news_drafts.headline: Three major schemes are 89–98% underspent: Leisure, Museum, Crematorium
news_drafts.lead: Multiple major capital projects with minimal progress at mid-year indicates systemic delivery constraints or unrealistic budget planning that will affect the council's capital strategy

news_drafts.headline: Greyfriars capital scheme is 97% underspent at mid-year
news_drafts.lead: Minimal progress on a multi-million pound capital project raises questions about scheme viability, planning obstacles, or market conditions that could jeopardise capital programme delivery
